original_question: In gamma-ray burst (GRB) studies, bursts have traditionally been classified as long/soft or short/hard using the duration measure T90, with about 2 seconds as a rough dividing line, together with spectral hardness. Because T90 depends on detector bandpass and sensitivity and does not always track the physical origin of a burst, what classification scheme should be used to map observed GRBs to physically meaningful progenitor classes such as massive-star (Type II) events versus compact-object-merger (Type I) events?
target_in_paper: Section 2.1 Classification notes that “since duration alone is no longer necessarily a good indicator for the physical category of a GRB, one must appeal to multiple observational criteria to judge the correct physical category of the GRB progenitor model that is associated with a certain GRB,” and that for GRBs with redshift measurements “a parameter can be used to classify GRBs into two categories” which map more closely to Type II (massive star) versus Type I (compact star) events.
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies that GRBs were traditionally classified by observer‐frame duration T90 (~2 s dividing line) and spectral hardness, and that this scheme is detector‐dependent and fails to track physical progenitors.
missing_details: Explicit definition of T90 (time interval containing 90% of counts, measured in a specified detector energy band)
Specification of detector bandpasses (e.g. BATSE 30–2000 keV versus Swift/BAT 15–150 keV) and sensitivity dependence
Definition of spectral hardness ratio and its energy channels
Clear statement of the physical progenitor classes: Type II (massive star collapse) and Type I (compact object merger)
List of the multiple observational criteria invoked (e.g. supernova association, host galaxy type, afterglow location and offset, spectral lag)
Mention of the redshift‐dependent classification parameter ε≡E_iso,52/E_p,z,2^{5/3} introduced by Lü et al. (2010) [42]
Quantification of how these criteria map to Type II versus Type I GRBs
Scope restriction to cosmological GRBs marking catastrophic explosions
Clarification that classification must be detector‐independent across GRB missions
refined_question: For cosmological gamma-ray bursts observed by instruments with different energy bandpasses and sensitivities (e.g. BATSE: 30–2000 keV; Swift/BAT: 15–150 keV), how can one construct a detector-independent, physically motivated classification scheme—beyond the traditional observer-frame T90 duration (>2 s vs <2 s) and spectral hardness ratio—that reliably assigns each GRB to its progenitor class of massive star collapse (Type II) versus compact object merger (Type I)? Specifically, which combination of multi-wavelength observational signatures (such as supernova association, host galaxy morphology, spectral lag, rest-frame peak energy E_p,z, isotropic energy E_iso) and redshift-dependent parameter ε≡E_iso,52/E_p,z,2^{5/3} should be adopted to map observed bursts to their physical origins?
justification: The draft captures the core issue from Section 2.1 that duration-based classification is flawed and that physical classification requires multiple criteria, but omits essential definitions (T90, hardness ratio, detector bandpasses), explicit progenitor class labels (Type I vs Type II), and the redshift-dependent parameter ε introduced in Ref. [42]. The refined question incorporates these details to be self-contained, tightly scoped to the paper’s open problem, and faithful to Zhang’s recommendation to use multiple observational criteria.
